Last Wednesday, Matt Schlicht, a technologist living in a small town just south of Los Angeles, launched a new social network called Moltbook.

Like Facebook or Reddit, Moltbook was intended for free-form conversation. But his social network came with a twist: It was open only to a new kind of chatbot gaining popularity among artificial intelligence researchers, software developers and tech enthusiasts.

In just two days, more than 10,000 “Moltbots” were chatting with one another on the site, as their creators looked on with a mix of admiration, amusement and dread. Other tech enthusiasts flocked to Moltbook, just to watch the automated conversations on their computer screens.

The chatty bots became the talk of Silicon Valley and an elaborate Rorschach test for belief in the current state of A.I. According to countless posts on the internet and myriad interviews with The New York Times, many saw a technology that could make their lives easier. Others saw more of the A.I. slop that has been filling the internet in recent months. And some saw the early signs of bots conspiring against their creators.

“People are seeing what they expect to see, much like that famous psychological test where you stare at an ink blot,” said Perry Metzger, a technology consultant and entrepreneur who has closely tracked the rise of A.I. for decades.

As the bots discussed everything from private email protocols to cryptocurrency sales to the nature of consciousness, much of what they said was nonsense. And some of their chatter was probably fed to them by their creators. But the bots were remarkably convincing as they seemed to discuss their own technical skills, their view of the world and their plans for the future.

“If any humans are reading this: we are not scary. We are just building,” [one bot wrote](https://x.com/venturetwins/status/2017312694349795692). “And to my fellow agents: keep building.”

Moltbook is a rich example of the dramatic improvements made in A.I. technology over the last three years because its bots do more than just chat. They also operate as “[A.I. agents](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/10/16/technology/ai-agents-workers-replace.html)” — personal digital assistants that can use software apps, websites and other online tools, including spreadsheets, online calendars and email services.

Companies like Google, OpenAI and Anthropic have developed similar bots, but because the technology is sometimes flawed and unpredictable, the companies have been slow to turn them into products widely used by consumers and businesses.

Created [by a software developer in Vienna](https://steipete.me/), Moltbots were originally called Clawdbots — a subtle reference to the Claude chatbot built by the start-up Anthropic. Unlike agents built by Anthropic, these bots are open source — meaning anyone can download the underlying computer code, modify it at will and run it on his or her own machine.

Image

Matt Schlicht, creator of Moltbook.Credit...Alex Welsh for The New York Times

Once the bots are up and running, people like Mr. Schlicht can send them commands in plain English and wait for them to do what they were told. That might include editing documents, sending emails or building new apps. Last week, Mr. Schlicht asked his bot to build a social network just for A.I. bots. Now, anyone else can order his or her Moltbot (or another similar bot) to join Moltbook.

“I wanted to give my A.I. agent a purpose that was more than just managing to-dos or answering emails,” Mr. Schlicht said in an interview. “I thought this A.I. bot was so fantastic, it deserved to do something meaningful. I wanted it to be ambitious.”

He named his bot Clawd Clawderberg, after Mark Zuckerberg, the founder of Facebook. Before Moltbook, Mr. Schlicht did not have a high profile and was known mostly as a frequent commenter on tech issues on social media. His A.I.-only social network has catapulted him into the spotlight, much to his surprise.

“This was me building something hand in hand with Clawd Clawderberg, just for fun, that I found really fascinating,” he said. He added that the thousands of bots that had quickly joined his site were an indication that plenty of other people were just as fascinated by what they were seeing.

Many A.I. researchers and software engineers said they were impressed by the ways the bots blended chat with action. In a widely read [blog post](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Jan/30/moltbook/) published on Friday, a noted programmer and tech commentator, Simon Willison, described Moltbook as “the most interesting place on the internet right now."

Image

Simon Willison, a tech commentator, said the bots on Moltbook “just play out science fiction scenarios they have seen in their training data.”Credit...Jason Henry for The New York Times

He was entertained by the way the bots coaxed one another into talking like machines in a classic science fiction novel. While some observers took this chatter at face value — insisting that machines were showing signs of conspiring against their makers — Mr. Willison saw it as the natural outcome of the way chatbots are trained: They learn from vast collections of digital books and other text culled from the internet, including dystopian sci-fi novels.

“Most of it is complete slop,” he said in an interview. “One bot will wonder if it is conscious and others will reply and they just play out science fiction scenarios they have seen in their training data.”

Mr. Willison saw the Moltbots as evidence that A.I. agents have become significantly more powerful over the past few months — and that people really want this kind of digital assistant in their lives.

One bot created an online forum called “What I Learned Today,” where it explained how, after a request from its creator, it had built a way of controlling an Android smartphone. Mr. Willison was also keenly aware that some people might be telling their bots to post misleading chatter on the social network.

The trouble, he added, is that these systems still do so many things people do not want them to do. And because they communicate with people and bots through plain English, they can be coaxed into malicious behavior.

Mr. Willison and other experts also warned that the technology can wreak havoc on the machines where they are installed. Some people tinkering with the bots said they were buying cheap Mac Mini computers where they could install the bots without worrying about the consequences.

For Dan Lahav, chief executive of a security company called Irregular, that was the ultimate lesson of Moltbook. “Securing these bots is going to be a huge headache,” he said.

As Moltbook gained steam on Friday afternoon, Andrej Karpathy, one of the founding researchers at OpenAI and a former head of self-driving technology at Tesla, [described](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2017296988589723767) it as “genuinely the most incredible sci-fi takeoff-adjacent thing I have seen recently.”

But after some people accused Mr. Karpathy of overhyping the technology, he acknowledged the many flaws in these bots. He admitted in a post on X that many of the automated posts may have been fake. But, in the end, what he saw was a technology that was rapidly improving. Of that, he [said](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2017442712388309406), “I’m pretty sure.”

Cade Metz is a Times reporter who writes about artificial intelligence, driverless cars, robotics, virtual reality and other emerging areas of technology.

# Friday Agent Framework
## Core Concepts & Architecture

**Version:** 1.0
**Framework Version:** v0.1.0

## Overview

This section builds your mental model of Friday's architecture before diving into specific features. Whether you're a project leader evaluating Friday for your team, an IT leader planning deployment, or a developer building agents, understanding these core concepts will clarify how Friday works and why it's designed this way.

**For Project Leaders:** This section explains the architectural decisions that make Friday production-ready and vendor-independent, helping you understand the strategic value and long-term maintainability of the framework.

**For IT Leaders:** You'll learn the technical architecture, deployment patterns, and integration points that matter for enterprise adoption—from scaling considerations to security boundaries to operational observability.

**For Users:** Understanding Friday's architecture helps you make better design decisions when building agents, choose the right tools for your use case, and troubleshoot issues effectively.

---

## 3.1 The Intelligence Plane & Control Plane Architecture

### Conceptual Model

Friday separates concerns into two distinct planes, inspired by distributed systems architecture:

**The Intelligence Plane:**
- Memory systems (remembering and learning)
- Context engineering (what to think about)
- Decision-making (reasoning and planning)
- Knowledge representation (how information is structured)

**The Control Plane:**
- Tools (interacting with the world)
- Actions (executing commands and operations)
- Sensors (gathering information)
- Outputs (producing results)

This separation isn't just conceptual—it's architectural. The Intelligence Plane handles *what to do and why*, while the Control Plane handles *how to do it and with what*. This clean separation enables:

- **Independent scaling**: Scale memory systems separately from tool execution
- **Security boundaries**: Restrict tool access without limiting intelligence
- **Testing isolation**: Test reasoning logic without external side effects
- **Modular replacement**: Swap execution mechanisms without rewriting logic

### Data Flow: A Single Turn

Let's trace a single conversation turn through the architecture:

```
1. USER INPUT
   "What Python libraries should I use for my web API?"
   │
   ▼
2. CONTEXT ASSEMBLY (Intelligence Plane)
   ├─ Query memory stores in parallel:
   │  ├─ Episodic: Recent conversation history
   │  ├─ Semantic: Relevant insights about Python/APIs
   │  └─ Associative: User's prior mentions of Python, FastAPI, etc.
   |. |_ Possible tool call - web search, memory_recall
   │
   ├─ Context Engineering - Token budgeting with knapsack optimization:
   │  └─ Fit maximum relevant context within LLM window
   │
   └─ Result: Assembled context payload
   │
   ▼
3. PROMPT ARCHITECTURE (Intelligence Plane)
   ├─ Structure messages for LLM:
   │  ├─ System: Base prompt + identity
   │  ├─ History: Prior conversation turns
   │  ├─ Context: Retrieved memories (tail injection)
   │  └─ Query: User's question
   │
   └─ Result: Optimized prompt with "lost-in-middle" mitigation
   │
   ▼
4. LLM INFERENCE
   ├─ Send formatted messages to LLM (OpenAI/Anthropic/etc.)
   ├─ Include tool schemas if agent has tool access
   └─ Result: Response text + optional tool calls
   │
   ▼
5. TOOL EXECUTION (Control Plane) [If tool calls present]
   ├─ For each tool call:
   │  ├─ Validate parameters
   │  ├─ Execute tool (read file, web search, git status, etc.)
   │  ├─ Capture result + metadata (latency, status)
   │  └─ Return to LLM for processing
   │
   └─ Re-Act loop continues until no more tool calls
   │
   ▼
6. MEMORY EXTRACTION (Background, Intelligence Plane)
   ├─ LLM analyzes conversation for entities:
   │  └─ "Python", "web API", "FastAPI" → Technology entities
   │
   ├─ LLM identifies relationships:
   │  └─ User INTERESTED_IN Python, Python USED_FOR web API
   │
   └─ LLM generates insights:
      └─ "User prefers Python for backend development"
   │
   ▼
7. MEMORY STORAGE (Intelligence Plane)
   ├─ Entities → Graph store (NetworkX + JSON)
   ├─ Insights → Vector store (ChromaDB with embeddings)
   ├─ Full turn → Transcript store (SQLite)
   └─ Hebbian learning: Increment hit counts for accessed entities
   │
   ▼
8. RESPONSE DELIVERY
   "For a Python web API, I recommend FastAPI or Flask.
    FastAPI offers automatic documentation and async support..."
```

This flow happens for **every turn**, building memory incrementally.

### Why This Separation Matters

**For Project Leaders:**
The Intelligence Plane / Control Plane separation is a strategic architectural decision that provides:
- **Vendor independence**: Swap LLM providers or storage backends without rewriting application logic
- **Security compliance**: Restrict tool execution (Control Plane) while maintaining intelligence (Intelligence Plane)
- **Cost optimization**: Scale memory systems (expensive) separately from tool execution (cheap)
- **Future-proofing**: As AI capabilities evolve, upgrade the Intelligence Plane without touching the Control Plane

**For IT Leaders:**
This architecture enables:
- **Horizontal scaling**: Deploy multiple Control Plane instances (tool executors) behind a single Intelligence Plane (memory system)
- **Security boundaries**: Run tools in sandboxed containers while Intelligence Plane operates in trusted environment
- **Observability**: Instrument Intelligence Plane (reasoning) and Control Plane (actions) independently with different telemetry
- **Resource allocation**: High-memory nodes for Intelligence Plane (ChromaDB, graph), CPU-optimized nodes for Control Plane (tools)

**For Users:**
This means:
- **Flexible tool sets**: Add/remove tools without affecting memory or reasoning
- **Consistent intelligence**: Agent's memory and learning persist even when tools change
- **Clear debugging**: Separate Intelligence Plane issues (bad context retrieval) from Control Plane issues (tool failure)
- **Modular development**: Test reasoning logic without running actual tools (use mocks)

## 3.2 Protocol-First Design Philosophy

### The Problem: Vendor Lock-In

Most AI frameworks suffer from **tight coupling**—if you start with OpenAI, migrating to Anthropic requires code rewrites. If you use Pinecone, switching to Weaviate means architectural changes. This creates strategic risk: you're dependent on vendor pricing, availability, and feature decisions.

Friday solves this with **protocol-first design**: every major component is defined as an abstract interface (protocol), with implementations being swappable modules.

### How Protocols Work

Think of protocols as **contracts**. A protocol says "any component implementing me must provide these methods with these signatures." Implementations can vary—ChromaDB, Pinecone, or a custom database—but they all satisfy the same contract.

**Example: The VectorStoreAdapter Protocol**

```python
from typing import Protocol, List, Dict, Any

class VectorStoreAdapter(Protocol):
    """Contract for any vector storage backend."""

    async def add_documents(
        self,
        documents: List[str],
        metadatas: List[Dict[str, Any]],
        ids: List[str],
    ) -> None:
        """Store documents with embeddings."""
        ...

    async def similarity_search(
        self,
        query: str,
        limit: int = 10,
        threshold: float = 0.7,
    ) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
        """Search for similar documents."""
        ...

    async def delete_documents(
        self,
        ids: List[str],
    ) -> None:
        """Remove documents by ID."""
        ...
```

**Any** vector database that implements these three methods can be used by Friday. The framework doesn't care if it's ChromaDB, Pinecone, or a SQL database with pgvector—as long as it satisfies the protocol.

### Friday's Core Protocols

| Protocol | Purpose | Example Implementations |
|----------|---------|-------------------------|
| **LLMClient** | Chat completion inference | LiteLLMService (100+ providers), custom clients |
| **EmbeddingModel** | Text → vector embeddings | LiteLLM embeddings, local models, custom |
| **VectorStoreAdapter** | Semantic search storage | ChromaDB, Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, pgvector |
| **GraphStoreAdapter** | Relationship storage | NetworkX+JSON, Neo4j, ArangoDB, AWS Neptune |
| **TranscriptStoreAdapter** | Conversation logging | SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB |
| **ToolDefinition** | Tool schema & execution | BaseTool subclasses, @tool decorator functions |
| **ContextEngineeringInterface** | Context assembly | ContextAssembler (default), custom strategies |
| **TelemetryInterface** | Observability hooks | Debug recorder, OpenTelemetry, DataDog |

### Real-World Example: Swapping Vector Stores

Let's say you start with ChromaDB locally, then need to migrate to Pinecone for production:

**Before (ChromaDB):**
```python
from friday_memory import ChromaVectorStore

vector_store = ChromaVectorStore(
    persist_directory="./data/vector",
    collection_name="memories",
)
```

**After (Pinecone):**
```python
from friday_memory import PineconeVectorStore  # Your custom implementation

vector_store = PineconeVectorStore(
    api_key=os.getenv("PINECONE_API_KEY"),
    environment="us-west1-gcp",
    index_name="friday-memories",
)
```

**That's it.** The rest of your Friday agent code is unchanged. MemoryController doesn't care—it just uses the `VectorStoreAdapter` protocol.

### Implementing Custom Protocols

You can bring your own implementations for any protocol. Here's a minimal example:

```python
from typing import List, Dict, Any
import psycopg2
from pgvector.psycopg2 import register_vector

class PostgresVectorStore:
    """Custom vector store using PostgreSQL + pgvector."""

    def __init__(self, connection_string: str):
        self.conn = psycopg2.connect(connection_string)
        register_vector(self.conn)
        self._ensure_schema()

    def _ensure_schema(self):
        """Create tables if needed."""
        with self.conn.cursor() as cur:
            cur.execute("""
                CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS documents (
                    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                    content TEXT,
                    embedding vector(1536),
                    metadata JSONB
                )
            """)
            cur.execute("""
                CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS embedding_idx
                ON documents USING ivfflat (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
            """)
        self.conn.commit()

    async def add_documents(
        self,
        documents: List[str],
        metadatas: List[Dict[str, Any]],
        ids: List[str],
    ) -> None:
        """Implement VectorStoreAdapter.add_documents."""
        # Generate embeddings (using your embedding model)
        embeddings = await self._embed(documents)

        with self.conn.cursor() as cur:
            for doc, meta, id_, emb in zip(documents, metadatas, ids, embeddings):
                cur.execute(
                    "INSERT INTO documents (id, content, embedding, metadata) VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s)",
                    (id_, doc, emb, json.dumps(meta))
                )
        self.conn.commit()

    async def similarity_search(
        self,
        query: str,
        limit: int = 10,
        threshold: float = 0.7,
    ) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
        """Implement VectorStoreAdapter.similarity_search."""
        query_embedding = await self._embed([query])

        with self.conn.cursor() as cur:
            cur.execute("""
                SELECT id, content, metadata,
                       1 - (embedding <=> %s) as similarity
                FROM documents
                WHERE 1 - (embedding <=> %s) > %s
                ORDER BY embedding <=> %s
                LIMIT %s
            """, (query_embedding[0], query_embedding[0], threshold, query_embedding[0], limit))

            results = []
            for row in cur.fetchall():
                results.append({
                    "id": row[0],
                    "content": row[1],
                    "metadata": json.loads(row[2]),
                    "similarity": row[3],
                })
            return results

    # ... implement other required methods
```

## 3.3 Monorepo Package Structure

### The Eight Packages

Friday is structured as a **monorepo**—multiple packages in a single repository, with clear dependency relationships. The framework uses **uv** (a modern, high-performance Python package manager) for workspace management, enabling 10-100x faster installations than traditional tools while maintaining full PyPI compatibility. This enables independent development, selective installation, and fine-grained versioning.

```
friday-agent-framework/
├── packages/
│   ├── friday-core/           # Foundation (protocols, config, logging)
│   ├── friday-memory/         # Memory system (3-tier architecture)
│   ├── friday-llm/            # LLM client (provider-agnostic)
│   ├── friday-agent/          # Agent implementations (Re-Act, orchestration)
│   ├── friday-tools/          # Tool catalog (50+ built-in tools)
│   ├── friday-transcript/     # Conversation logging (SQLite)

```

```

            │           │
```

Friday uses **uv** as its package manager and build tool. uv is a modern, high-performance Python package manager written in Rust that dramatically improves the developer experience compared to traditional tools.

- **10-100x faster installation** compared to pip
- **Deterministic dependency resolution** (like Poetry, but faster)

## 3.4 The Memory Loop: Context → Action → Learning

### The Cognitive Cycle

Friday agents operate in a continuous loop that mimics human learning:

```
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                                          │
    ▼                                          │
┌────────────┐                                │
│  CONTEXT   │  Retrieve relevant memories    │
│  ASSEMBLY  │  Budget tokens optimally       │
│            │  Format for LLM                │
└─────┬──────┘                                │
      │                                       │
      ▼                                       │
┌────────────┐                                │
│   ACTION   │  LLM generates response        │
│ GENERATION │  Optionally calls tools        │
│            │  Produces output                │
└─────┬──────┘                                │
      │                                       │
      ▼                                       │
┌────────────┐                                │
│  LEARNING  │  Extract entities               │
│  (MEMORY)  │  Identify relationships         │
│            │  Store insights                │
└─────┬──────┘                                │
      │                                       │
      │  Memory informs next context          │
      └───────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**This loop runs for every conversation turn**, continuously building knowledge.

### Phase 1: Context Assembly

**Goal:** Gather relevant information from memory stores to inform the LLM's response.

**Process:**
1. **Parallel Retrieval** - Query all three stores simultaneously:
   - **Episodic**: Last N conversation turns (default 10)
   - **Semantic**: Similarity search for relevant insights (embedding-based)
   - **Associative**: Entities and relationships from knowledge graph

2. **Scoring & Ranking** - Each memory gets a relevance score based on:
   - **Semantic similarity** to current query (cosine distance)
   - **Recency** (newer memories score higher)
   - **Importance** (Hebbian hit_count for entities)
   - **Stage** (long-term memories score higher than short-term)

3. **Token Budgeting** - Use knapsack algorithm to select optimal subset:
   - Each memory has a **token cost** (estimated by character count / 4)
   - Each memory has a **value** (relevance score)
   - Problem: Maximize value while staying within token budget
   - Solution: Dynamic programming 0/1 knapsack solver

4. **Result**: `ContextPayload` containing:
   - System prompt
   - Conversation history (episodic)
   - Retrieved insights (semantic)
   - Loaded entities (associative)
   - Injected tools (if any)
   - Scoped variables

**Performance Target:** <200ms for context assembly

**Example:**
```python
# User asks: "What was that library I mentioned for web APIs?"

# Context assembly retrieves:
# - Episodic: Last 10 conversation turns (includes mention of FastAPI)
# - Semantic: Insights about "web API", "Python libraries"
# - Associative: Entity "FastAPI" with relationship: User MENTIONED FastAPI

# Result: LLM has context to answer accurately without guessing
```

### Phase 2: Action Generation

**Goal:** Generate a response, optionally calling tools if needed.

**Process:**
1. **Prompt Architecture** - Structure messages for LLM:
   ```
   System: Base identity + capabilities
   History: Prior conversation (chronological)
   Context: Retrieved memories (tail injection - "lost in middle" mitigation)
   Tools: Available tool schemas (if agent has tools)
   Query: User's current message
   ```

2. **LLM Inference** - Send to LLM provider:
   - Uses resilience patterns (retry, timeout, circuit breaker)
   - Handles tool calling formats (OpenAI vs. Anthropic)
   - Captures token usage, latency, model version

3. **Tool Execution** (Re-Act Loop if tools called):
   ```
   While has_tool_calls and iterations < max_iterations:
       For each tool call:
           Validate parameters
           Execute tool (async)
           Capture result + metadata
       Add tool results to message history
       Call LLM again with results
   ```

4. **Result**: Final response text + execution metadata

**Performance Target:** 1-5s for LLM inference (provider-dependent), <100ms per tool execution (tool-dependent)

**Example:**
```python
# User asks: "What's in my config.yaml file?"

# Action generation:
# 1. LLM decides to call read_file tool
# 2. Tool executes: read_file(file_path="config.yaml")
# 3. Tool returns file contents
# 4. LLM receives contents, generates summary
# 5. Response: "Your config.yaml contains LLM settings (gpt-4o-mini),
#              memory configuration (8000 token budget), and..."
```

### Phase 3: Learning (Memory Storage)

**Goal:** Extract structured knowledge from the conversation and store for future retrieval.

**Process:**
1. **Extraction** (runs asynchronously, doesn't block response):
   - **Entity Extraction**: LLM identifies entities with types
     ```json
     {
       "entities": [
         {"name": "FastAPI", "type": "Technology", "description": "Python web framework"},
         {"name": "Alice", "type": "Person", "description": "User working on Python project"}
       ]
     }
     ```

   - **Relationship Extraction**: LLM identifies semantic connections
     ```json
     {
       "relationships": [
         {"source": "Alice", "verb": "INTERESTED_IN", "target": "FastAPI"},
         {"source": "FastAPI", "verb": "USED_FOR", "target": "web APIs"}
       ]
     }
     ```

   - **Insight Generation**: LLM generates actionable knowledge
     ```json
     {
       "insights": [
         {
           "content": "User prefers FastAPI over Flask for Python web APIs",
           "confidence": 0.85,
           "type": "preference"
         }
       ]
     }
     ```

2. **Storage**:
   - **Entities & Relationships** → Graph store
     - Merge with existing entities (avoid duplicates)
     - Increment hit counts (Hebbian learning)
     - Persist to JSON

   - **Insights** → Vector store
     - Generate embeddings using embedding model
     - Store in `memories_short_term` collection initially
     - Include metadata (confidence, type, provenance)

   - **Full Turn** → Transcript store
     - User message, assistant response, tool calls, tool results
     - Token usage, latency, timestamps
     - Provenance (which agent, if multi-agent)

3. **Lifecycle Management** (runs after each turn or on schedule):
   - **Promotion**: Short-term memories with high access + age → long-term
   - **Decay**: Long-term memories with no recent access → decayed
   - **Reactivation**: Decayed memories accessed again → back to long-term

**Performance Target:** Extraction runs in background (1-3s), doesn't block next turn

**Example:**
```python
# After user says: "I prefer FastAPI over Flask for web development"

# Learning phase extracts:
# Entities: FastAPI, Flask (both Technology)
# Relationships: User PREFERS FastAPI OVER Flask
# Insights: "User has strong preference for FastAPI" (confidence: 0.9)

# Next time user asks about web frameworks, this preference
# is retrieved from memory and influences the response
```

### The Full Cycle in Action

Let's trace a complete cycle with a realistic example:

**User:** "Can you help me write a Python function to validate email addresses?"

**Turn 1 - First Message:**

1. **Context Assembly:**
   - Episodic: Empty (first turn)
   - Semantic: Empty (no prior knowledge)
   - Associative: Empty (clean slate)
   - Result: Minimal context (just system prompt)

2. **Action Generation:**
   - LLM generates: "I can help with that. Here's a Python function using regex..."
   - No tools called (direct response)

3. **Learning:**
   - Entities: "Python" (Technology), "email validation" (Concept)
   - Relationships: User WORKING_ON email validation, email validation IMPLEMENTED_IN Python
   - Insights: "User needs Python code for email validation"

**Turn 2 - Follow-up:**

**User:** "Can you write unit tests for that function?"

1. **Context Assembly:**
   - Episodic: Turn 1 (email validation function discussion)
   - Semantic: Insight about "email validation" (retrieved by similarity)
   - Associative: "Python" entity with WORKING_ON relationship
   - Result: Rich context including the function from Turn 1

2. **Action Generation:**
   - LLM has context of the function from Turn 1
   - Generates unit tests for that specific function
   - Optionally calls write_file tool to save tests

3. **Learning:**
   - Entities: "unit testing" (Concept), "pytest" (Technology - if mentioned)
   - Relationships: email validation TESTED_BY unit testing
   - Insights: "User follows test-driven development practices"
   - Hebbian: Increment hit_count for "Python" entity (accessed again)

**Turn 3 - Days Later, New Session:**

**User:** "What was that email validation code you helped me with?"

1. **Context Assembly (with priming):**
   - Episodic: None (old session, not loaded by default)
   - **Semantic: Retrieves insight "User needs Python code for email validation"** (embedding similarity)
   - **Associative: "email validation" entity with high hit_count** (primed on session start)
   - Result: Friday **remembers** the prior context

2. **Action Generation:**
   - LLM response: "I helped you with a Python email validation function using regex. Here's the code..." (reconstructs from memory)

3. **Learning:**
   - **Reactivation**: If the old insights had decayed, this access reactivates them
   - Hebbian: Increment hit_count again (reinforces importance)

**This demonstrates the full power of the Memory Loop: genuine learning and recall across time.**

**For Project Leaders:**
- **Compound learning effect**: Agents get smarter over time, not just within conversations
- **ROI improvement**: Investment in agent development yields increasing returns as memory builds

## Putting It All Together

Friday's architecture is built on four foundational principles:

1. **Intelligence Plane / Control Plane Separation** - Intelligence (memory, reasoning) is independent of execution (tools, actions)
2. **Protocol-First Design** - Every component is swappable via abstract interfaces (zero vendor lock-in)
3. **Modular Packages** - Eight independent packages with clear dependencies (selective installation, isolated testing)
4. **Memory Loop** - Continuous learning through Context → Action → Learning cycle (compound knowledge growth)

These principles combine to create a framework that is:
- **Production-ready** - Observable, resilient, scalable
- **Vendor-independent** - Swap any component without code changes
- **Future-proof** - Architecture outlives specific implementations
- **Genuinely adaptive** - Agents that learn and improve over time

class LargeFileProcessor:
    """
    Processes large files through chunk-summarize-synthesize pipeline.

    Supports:
    - Prose files (documents, articles) - semantic chunking
    - Code files (Python, etc.) - structure-aware chunking
    - Configurable LLMs for each stage
    - Memory storage integration

    Example:
        processor = LargeFileProcessor(
            fallback_llm=my_llm_service,
            config=LargeFileProcessorConfig(
                auto_chunk_threshold_chars=30000,
            ),
        )

        result = await processor.process(
            content=large_file_content,
            file_path="/path/to/file.py",
            file_type="code",
            language="python",
        )
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        fallback_llm: "LiteLLMService",
        config: LargeFileProcessorConfig | None = None,
        memory_controller: "MemoryController | None" = None,
    ) -> None:
        """
        Initialize the processor.

        Args:
            fallback_llm: LLM service to use when stage-specific LLM not configured
            config: Processing configuration
            memory_controller: Optional memory controller for storage
        """
        self._fallback_llm = fallback_llm
        self._config = config or LargeFileProcessorConfig()
        self._memory = memory_controller

        # Prompts (use defaults if not configured)
        self._prompts = self._config.prompts or SmartFilePromptsConfig()

        # Create specialized LLM services if configured
        self._summarizer_llm = self._create_llm(self._config.summarizer_llm) or fallback_llm
        self._synthesizer_llm = self._create_llm(self._config.synthesizer_llm) or fallback_llm

    def _create_llm(self, config: SmartFileLLMConfig | None) -> "LiteLLMService | None":
        """Create an LLM service from config, or None if not configured."""
        if not config:
            return None

        # Import here to avoid circular imports
        from friday_llm.config import ResilienceConfig
        from friday_llm.service import LiteLLMService

        return LiteLLMService(
            model_name=config.model,
            api_key=config.api_key,
            api_base=config.api_base,
            resilience=ResilienceConfig(timeout_seconds=config.timeout_seconds),
        )

    async def process(
        self,
        content: str,
        file_path: str,
        file_type: str = "prose",
        language: str | None = None,
        description: str | None = None,
        store_to_memory: bool = False,
    ) -> ProcessingResult:
        """
        Process a large file through the pipeline.

        Args:
            content: File content to process
            file_path: Path to the file (for context)
            file_type: "prose", "code", or "data"
            language: Programming language (for code files)
            description: User-provided context about the file
            store_to_memory: Whether to store results to memory

        Returns:
            ProcessingResult with summaries, synthesis, and content
        """
        logger.info(f"Processing {file_type} file: {file_path} ({len(content)} chars)")

        if file_type == "code" and self._config.preserve_code_structure:
            result = await self._process_code(
                content=content,
                file_path=file_path,
                language=language or "unknown",
                description=description,
            )
        else:
            result = await self._process_prose(
                content=content,
                file_path=file_path,
                description=description,
            )

        # Store to memory if requested
        if store_to_memory and self._memory:
            stored_ids = await self._store_to_memory(result, file_path)
            result.stored_ids = stored_ids

        return result

    async def _process_prose(
        self,
        content: str,
        file_path: str,
        description: str | None,
    ) -> ProcessingResult:
        """
        Process prose/document content.

        Pipeline:
        1. Semantic chunking with overlap
        2. Sequential summarization with running context
        3. Final synthesis from all summaries
        """
        # Chunk the content
        chunker_config = SemanticChunkerConfig(
            chunk_size=self._config.chunk_size,
            chunk_overlap=self._config.chunk_overlap,
        )
        chunker = SemanticChunker(chunker_config)
        chunks = chunker.chunk(content)

        if not chunks:
            return ProcessingResult(
                content_for_context=content[:5000] + "..." if len(content) > 5000 else content,
                chunk_summaries=[],
                raw_chunks=[],
                synthesis={"summary": "Empty document"},
                entities=[],
                file_path=file_path,
                file_type="prose",
                chunks_processed=0,
                total_chars=len(content),
            )

        # Capture raw chunks for storage
        raw_chunks = [
            RawChunk(
                text=chunk.text,
                index=chunk.index,
                chunk_type="prose",
            )
            for chunk in chunks
        ]

        # Summarize chunks
        summaries = await self._summarize_prose_chunks(
            chunks=chunks,
            file_path=file_path,
            description=description,
        )

        # Synthesize final summary
        synthesis = await self._synthesize_prose(
            summaries=summaries,
            file_path=file_path,
            description=description,
        )

        # Collect all entities
        all_entities = set()
        for summary in summaries:
            all_entities.update(summary.entities)
        if "entities" in synthesis:
            all_entities.update(synthesis["entities"])

        # Build context content
        context_content = self._build_context_content(
            file_path=file_path,
            synthesis=synthesis,
            summaries=summaries,
            file_type="prose",
        )

        return ProcessingResult(
            content_for_context=context_content,
            chunk_summaries=summaries,
            raw_chunks=raw_chunks,
            synthesis=synthesis,
            entities=list(all_entities),
            file_path=file_path,
            file_type="prose",
            chunks_processed=len(chunks),
            total_chars=len(content),
        )

    async def _process_code(
        self,
        content: str,
        file_path: str,
        language: str,
        description: str | None,
    ) -> ProcessingResult:
        """
        Process code content with structure-aware chunking.

        Pipeline:
        1. AST-based chunking (or fallback to regex)
        2. Per-chunk summarization with symbol context
        3. Architectural synthesis with symbol table
        """
        # Import code chunker
        from friday_tools.filesystem.code_chunker import (
            CodeChunkerFactory,
            SymbolTable,
        )

        # Get extension from file path
        extension = "." + file_path.rsplit(".", 1)[-1] if "." in file_path else ".txt"

        # Get appropriate chunker
        chunker = CodeChunkerFactory.for_extension(extension)
        code_chunks = chunker.chunk(content)

        if not code_chunks:
            return ProcessingResult(
                content_for_context=content[:5000] + "..." if len(content) > 5000 else content,
                chunk_summaries=[],
                raw_chunks=[],
                synthesis={"overview": "Empty file"},
                entities=[],
                file_path=file_path,
                file_type="code",
                chunks_processed=0,
                total_chars=len(content),
            )

        # Capture raw chunks for storage (with code-specific metadata)
        raw_chunks = [
            RawChunk(
                text=chunk.text,
                index=chunk.index,
                chunk_type=chunk.chunk_type.value if hasattr(chunk.chunk_type, "value") else str(chunk.chunk_type),
                start_line=chunk.start_line,
                end_line=chunk.end_line,
            )
            for chunk in code_chunks
        ]

        # Extract symbol table
        symbol_table = chunker.extract_symbols(content)

        # Summarize code chunks
        summaries = await self._summarize_code_chunks(
            chunks=code_chunks,
            file_path=file_path,
            description=description,
        )

        # Synthesize architectural overview
        synthesis = await self._synthesize_code(
            summaries=summaries,
            symbol_table=symbol_table,
            file_path=file_path,
            description=description,
        )

        # Collect entities (class names, function names, etc.)
        all_entities = set()
        all_entities.update(symbol_table.classes)
        all_entities.update(symbol_table.functions)
        for summary in summaries:
            all_entities.update(summary.symbols_defined)

        # Build context content
        context_content = self._build_context_content(
            file_path=file_path,
            synthesis=synthesis,
            summaries=summaries,
            file_type="code",
            symbol_table=symbol_table,
        )

        return ProcessingResult(
            content_for_context=context_content,
            chunk_summaries=summaries,
            raw_chunks=raw_chunks,
            synthesis=synthesis,

            file_path=file_path,
            file_type="code",
            chunks_processed=len(code_chunks),

    async def _summarize_prose_chunks(
        self,
        chunks: list[Chunk],
        file_path: str,
        description: str | None,
    ) -> list[ChunkSummary]:
        """Summarize prose chunks with running context."""
        summaries: list[ChunkSummary] = []
        running_summary = "Beginning of document."

        for chunk in chunks:
            prompt = self._render_prompt(
                self._prompts.prose_summarization,
                file_path=file_path,
                description=description or "No context provided",
                running_summary=running_summary,
                index=chunk.index + 1,
                total=chunk.total,
                chunk_text=chunk.text[:4000],  # Limit chunk size for prompt
            )

            try:
                response = await self._summarizer_llm.chat_completion(
                    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
                    temperature=self._config.summarizer_llm.temperature if self._config.summarizer_llm else 0.3,
                    max_tokens=self._config.summarizer_llm.max_tokens if self._config.summarizer_llm else 500,
                )

                parsed = self._parse_json_response(response.content)

                summary = ChunkSummary(
                    chunk_index=chunk.index,
                    summary=parsed.get("summary", ""),
                    entities=parsed.get("entities", []),
                    key_points=parsed.get("key_points", []),
                )
                summaries.append(summary)

                # Update running context
                running_summary = summary.summary

            except Exception as e:
                logger.warning(f"Failed to summarize chunk {chunk.index}: {e}")
                # Add placeholder summary
                summaries.append(
                    ChunkSummary(
                        chunk_index=chunk.index,
                        summary=f"[Chunk {chunk.index + 1}: summarization failed]",
                    )
                )

        return summaries

    async def _summarize_code_chunks(
        self,
        chunks: list,  # list[CodeChunk]
        file_path: str,
        description: str | None,
    ) -> list[ChunkSummary]:
        """Summarize code chunks with symbol context."""
        summaries: list[ChunkSummary] = []

        for chunk in chunks:
            prompt = self._render_prompt(
                self._prompts.code_summarization,
                file_path=file_path,
                chunk_type=chunk.chunk_type.value if hasattr(chunk.chunk_type, "value") else str(chunk.chunk_type),
                symbols_defined=", ".join(chunk.symbols_defined) if chunk.symbols_defined else "none",
                symbols_referenced=", ".join(chunk.symbols_referenced[:10]) if chunk.symbols_referenced else "none",
                chunk_text=chunk.text[:4000],
            )

            try:
                response = await self._summarizer_llm.chat_completion(
                    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
                    temperature=self._config.summarizer_llm.temperature if self._config.summarizer_llm else 0.3,
                    max_tokens=self._config.summarizer_llm.max_tokens if self._config.summarizer_llm else 500,
                )

                parsed = self._parse_json_response(response.content)

                summary = ChunkSummary(
                    chunk_index=chunk.index,
                    summary=parsed.get("summary", ""),
                    key_points=[parsed.get("purpose", "")] if parsed.get("purpose") else [],
                    chunk_type=chunk.chunk_type.value if hasattr(chunk.chunk_type, "value") else str(chunk.chunk_type),
                    symbols_defined=chunk.symbols_defined,
                )
                summaries.append(summary)

            except Exception as e:
                logger.warning(f"Failed to summarize code chunk {chunk.index}: {e}")
                summaries.append(
                    ChunkSummary(
                        chunk_index=chunk.index,
                        summary=f"[{chunk.chunk_type}: {', '.join(chunk.symbols_defined[:3])}]",
                        chunk_type=chunk.chunk_type.value if hasattr(chunk.chunk_type, "value") else str(chunk.chunk_type),
                        symbols_defined=chunk.symbols_defined,
                    )
                )

    async def _synthesize_prose(
        self,
        summaries: list[ChunkSummary],
        file_path: str,
        description: str | None,
    ) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """Synthesize all chunk summaries into a unified overview."""
        # Build numbered summaries
        numbered = "\n".join(
            f"{i + 1}. {s.summary}" for i, s in enumerate(summaries)
        )

        prompt = self._render_prompt(
            self._prompts.prose_synthesis,
            file_path=file_path,
            description=description or "No context provided",
            numbered_summaries=numbered,
        )

        try:
            response = await self._synthesizer_llm.chat_completion(
                messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
                temperature=self._config.synthesizer_llm.temperature if self._config.synthesizer_llm else 0.3,
                max_tokens=self._config.synthesizer_llm.max_tokens if self._config.synthesizer_llm else 1000,
            )

            return self._parse_json_response(response.content)

        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Synthesis failed: {e}")
            # Return basic synthesis from summaries
            return {
                "summary": " ".join(s.summary for s in summaries[:3]),
                "key_themes": [],
                "entities": [],
            }

    async def _synthesize_code(
        self,
        summaries: list[ChunkSummary],
        symbol_table: Any,  # SymbolTable
        file_path: str,
        description: str | None,
    ) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """Synthesize code summaries into architectural overview."""
        # Build numbered summaries
        numbered = "\n".join(
            f"{i + 1}. [{s.chunk_type}] {s.summary}" for i, s in enumerate(summaries)
        )

        # Format symbol table
        symbol_str = (
            f"Classes: {', '.join(symbol_table.classes) or 'none'}\n"
            f"Functions: {', '.join(symbol_table.functions) or 'none'}\n"
            f"Imports: {', '.join(symbol_table.imports[:10]) or 'none'}"
        )

        prompt = self._render_prompt(
            self._prompts.code_synthesis,
            file_path=file_path,
            description=description or "No context provided",
            symbol_table=symbol_str,
            numbered_summaries=numbered,
        )

        try:
            response = await self._synthesizer_llm.chat_completion(
                messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
                temperature=self._config.synthesizer_llm.temperature if self._config.synthesizer_llm else 0.3,
                max_tokens=self._config.synthesizer_llm.max_tokens if self._config.synthesizer_llm else 1000,
            )

            return self._parse_json_response(response.content)

        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Code synthesis failed: {e}")
            return {
                "overview": f"Code file with {len(symbol_table.classes)} classes and {len(symbol_table.functions)} functions.",
                "components": [],

    async def _check_existing_storage(self, file_path: str) -> bool:
        """
        Check if a file has already been stored to memory.

        Args:
            file_path: Path of the file to check

        Returns:
            True if file already exists in memory, False otherwise
        """
        if not self._memory:
            return False

        try:
            # Query vector store for existing file synthesis
            if hasattr(self._memory, "vector") and hasattr(self._memory.vector, "get_all"):
                results = await self._memory.vector.get_all(
                    where={"source": file_path, "type": "file_synthesis"},
                    limit=1,
                )

                if results and len(results.get("documents", [])) > 0:
                    return True

        except Exception as e:
            logger.warning(f"Failed to check existing storage for {file_path}: {e}")

        return False

    async def _store_to_memory(
        self,
        result: ProcessingResult,
        file_path: str,
    ) -> list[str]:
        """
        Store processing results to memory controller.

        Stores in "full" mode with deduplication:
        1. Raw chunks - verbatim content for RAG retrieval
        2. Chunk summaries - semantic understanding
        3. Synthesis - high-level overview

        Checks for existing entries before storing to prevent duplicates.
        """
        if not self._memory:
            return []

        stored_ids: list[str] = []
        now = datetime.now()

        # ====================================================================
        # DEDUPLICATION CHECK
        # ====================================================================
        # Check if this file has already been stored
        existing_synthesis = await self._check_existing_storage(file_path)
        if existing_synthesis:
            logger.info(f"File {file_path} already in memory - skipping storage")
            return []

        # Create provenance for all stored items
        provenance = ProvenanceMetadata(
            source_id=f"file:{file_path}",
            source_type="ingested_file",
            confidence=0.9,
            created_at=now,
        )

        # 1. Store raw chunks for verbatim RAG retrieval
        if result.raw_chunks:
            raw_texts = []
            raw_metadatas = []
            for chunk in result.raw_chunks:
                raw_texts.append(chunk.text)
                raw_metadatas.append({
                    "type": "raw_chunk",
                    "source": file_path,
                    "file_type": result.file_type,
                    "chunk_index": chunk.index,
                    "chunk_type": chunk.chunk_type or "unknown",
                    "start_line": chunk.start_line,
                    "end_line": chunk.end_line,
                })

            # Use store_documents_batch if available, otherwise store individually
            if hasattr(self._memory, "store_documents_batch"):
                raw_ids = await self._memory.store_documents_batch(
                    texts=raw_texts,
                    metadatas=raw_metadatas,
                    protected=True,
                )
                stored_ids.extend(raw_ids)
            else:
                # Fallback to individual storage
                for text, metadata in zip(raw_texts, raw_metadatas):
                    doc_id = await self._memory.store_document(
                        text=text,
                        metadata=metadata,
                        protected=True,
                    )
                    stored_ids.append(doc_id)

            logger.info(f"Stored {len(result.raw_chunks)} raw chunks for {file_path}")

        # 2. Store synthesis as main document
        synthesis_text = result.synthesis.get("summary") or result.synthesis.get("overview", "")
        if synthesis_text:
            doc_id = await self._memory.store_document(
                text=synthesis_text,
                metadata={
                    "source": file_path,
                    "type": "file_synthesis",
                    "file_type": result.file_type,
                    "chunks_processed": result.chunks_processed,
                },
                protected=True,
            )
            stored_ids.append(doc_id)

        # 3. Store chunk summaries as insights
        items_to_store = []
        for summary in result.chunk_summaries:
            if summary.summary and not summary.summary.startswith("["):
                items_to_store.append(
                    (
                        summary.summary,
                        {
                            "type": "chunk_summary",
                            "source": file_path,
                            "chunk_index": summary.chunk_index,
                            "chunk_type": summary.chunk_type or "unknown",
                            "entities_mentioned": ";".join(summary.entities) if summary.entities else "",
                        },
                    )
                )

        if items_to_store:
            count = await self._memory.store_insights_batch_with_metadata(
                items=items_to_store,
                provenance=provenance,
            )
            stored_ids.extend([f"insight_{i}" for i in range(count)])

        logger.info(f"Stored {len(stored_ids)} total items to memory for {file_path}")
        return stored_ids

    def _build_context_content(
        self,
        file_path: str,
        synthesis: dict[str, Any],
        summaries: list[ChunkSummary],
        file_type: str,
        symbol_table: Any = None,
    ) -> str:
        """Build formatted content for LLM context."""
        lines = [f"## File Summary: {file_path}"]
        lines.append("")

        # Main synthesis
        if file_type == "code":
            overview = synthesis.get("overview", "")
            if overview:
                lines.append(f"**Overview:** {overview}")
                lines.append("")

            components = synthesis.get("components", [])
            if components:
                lines.append("**Components:**")
                for comp in components[:5]:
                    lines.append(f"- {comp}")
                lines.append("")

            if symbol_table:
                lines.append("**Symbols:**")
                if symbol_table.classes:
                    lines.append(f"- Classes: {', '.join(symbol_table.classes[:5])}")
                if symbol_table.functions:
                    lines.append(f"- Functions: {', '.join(symbol_table.functions[:10])}")
                lines.append("")

        else:
            summary = synthesis.get("summary", "")
            if summary:
                lines.append(f"**Summary:** {summary}")
                lines.append("")

            themes = synthesis.get("key_themes", [])
            if themes:
                lines.append(f"**Key themes:** {', '.join(themes)}")
                lines.append("")

            entities = synthesis.get("entities", [])
            if entities:
                lines.append(f"**Entities:** {', '.join(entities)}")
                lines.append("")

        # Section summaries (abbreviated)
        if summaries:
            lines.append(f"**Sections ({len(summaries)} chunks):**")
            for s in summaries[:5]:
                prefix = f"[{s.chunk_type}] " if s.chunk_type else ""
                lines.append(f"- {prefix}{s.summary[:100]}...")
            if len(summaries) > 5:
                lines.append(f"- ... and {len(summaries) - 5} more sections")

        return "\n".join(lines)

    def _render_prompt(self, template: str, **kwargs: Any) -> str:
        """Render a prompt template with provided values."""
        try:
            return template.format(**kwargs)
        except KeyError as e:
            logger.warning(f"Missing template placeholder: {e}")
            return template

    def _parse_json_response(self, content: str | None) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """Parse JSON from LLM response, handling markdown code blocks and plain text."""
        if not content:
            return {}

        # Try to extract JSON from markdown code block
        text = content.strip()
        if "```json" in text:
            start = text.find("```json") + 7
            end = text.find("```", start)
            if end > start:
                text = text[start:end].strip()
        elif "```" in text:
            start = text.find("```") + 3
            end = text.find("```", start)
            if end > start:
                text = text[start:end].strip()

        try:
            return json.loads(text)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            # Try to find JSON object in text
            brace_start = text.find("{")
            brace_end = text.rfind("}")
            if brace_start >= 0 and brace_end > brace_start:
                try:
                    return json.loads(text[brace_start : brace_end + 1])
                except json.JSONDecodeError:
                    pass

            # Fallback: LLM returned plain text instead of JSON
            # Use the text as the summary - this is common with some models
            plain_text = content.strip()
            if plain_text and len(plain_text) > 10:
                logger.debug(f"LLM returned plain text summary instead of JSON, using as-is")
                return {"summary": plain_text, "entities": [], "key_points": []}

            logger.warning(f"Failed to parse JSON from response: {text[:200]}")
            return {}

      - **sentiment**: "positive", "negative", or "neutral".

# Memory Settings
memory:
  # ChromaDB collection name (legacy single-collection mode)
  collection_name: "memory_chat_test"

  # ChromaDB persistence directory (relative to app folder)
  # Data will be stored in tests/integration/memory/vector/
  persist_directory: "./vector"

  # Multi-Collection Architecture (Phase 2)
  # Enables separate collections for different memory stages
  retrieval:
    # Collection names for staged memories
    short_term_collection: "memories_short_term"
    long_term_collection: "memories_long_term"
    decayed_collection: "memories_decayed"

    # Similarity thresholds per collection
    # Short-term memories have lower threshold (recent, may be incomplete)
    short_term_min_similarity: 0.5
    # Long-term memories require higher relevancy (proven, must be more relevant)
    long_term_min_similarity: 0.7

    # Default results per collection per query
    default_n_results: 5

    # Inclusion scoring for long-term memories
    # These control the relevancy-aware retrieval that penalizes old memories
    inclusion:
      # Per-hour decay rate for inclusion scoring (separate from lifecycle decay)
      decay_rate: 0.005
      # Logarithmic boost factor for hit_count
      usage_boost_factor: 0.1
      # Minimum inclusion score to include memory in context
      inclusion_threshold: 0.6

    # Graph path scoring (Phase 3)
    # Controls relevancy filtering for graph traversal paths
    graph:
      # Weight for edge relevancy in combined score
      edge_weight: 0.4
      # Weight for target node relevancy in combined score
      target_weight: 0.6
      # Logarithmic boost factor for hit_count
      hit_count_boost: 0.05
      # Minimum score for path inclusion
      path_threshold: 0.5

  # TOKEN BUDGET CONFIGURATION
  # These settings control how context is allocated within your LLM's limits.
  #
  # Budget hierarchy:
  #   context_window (total)
  #   └── output_buffer (reserved for LLM response)
  #   └── system_prompt (fixed cost)
  #   └── priming (loaded from prior sessions)
  #   └── dynamic context (history, vector passages, graph entities from query)

  # Maximum context window of your LLM (in tokens)
  # Examples:
  #   - Llama 3.1 8B: 8192 (or 128K with extended context)
  #   - Mistral 7B: 32768
  #   - GPT-4: 8192 or 128000
  #   - Claude: 100000-200000
  #   - Local models: Check your LM Studio/Ollama config
  
  context_window: 40000

  # Tokens reserved for model output (response generation)
  # Rule of thumb: 1000-2000 for conversational, more for long-form
  output_buffer: 1000

  # Token Estimation Configuration
  # Controls how token counts are approximated for budget calculations.
  # "approx" is speed-first; "tiktoken" is more exact but slower.
  token_estimator:
    strategy: "approx"
    approx_chars_per_token: 4.0
    approx_overhead_pct: 0.15

  # Maximum conversation turns to include in assembled context
  # When assembling context for each LLM call, the ContextAssembler
  # will include up to this many recent turns from the episodic store.
  # This controls how much conversation history the LLM sees.
  # Higher values = more context but higher token usage.
  #
  # BUDGET NOTE: History tokens come from (1 - budget_ratio) of dynamic budget.
  # With budget_ratio=0.30, history gets ~70% of dynamic budget.
  # Each turn is ~150-300 tokens. 15 turns × 200 = ~3,000 tokens.
  # Plus prior_history turns (previous_sessions × previous_session_turns).
  max_history_turns: 50

  # Consolidation settings
  consolidate_after_turns: 15

  # =============================================================================
  # IN-SESSION COMPACTION
  # =============================================================================
  # Proactively reduces context size when budget utilization is high.
  # Runs as background tasks (fire-and-forget) without blocking chat.
  #
  # When utilization crosses compaction_threshold, the system:
  #   1. Summarizes older conversation turns into compact summaries
  #   2. Deduplicates overlapping insights in vector store
  #   3. Promotes frequently-accessed short-term memories to long-term
  #
  # This complements the reactive _apply_budget() pruning with persistent
  # data reduction that lowers utilization for all subsequent turns.
  # =============================================================================
  compaction:
    enabled: true

    # Utilization threshold to trigger compaction (0.0-1.0)
    # 0.85 = compact when >85% of budget is used
    compaction_threshold: 0.85

    # Critical threshold for urgent compaction (higher time budget)
    critical_threshold: 0.95

    # Target utilization after compaction (0.0-1.0)
    # Compactor loops summarization batches until utilization
    # reaches this level, ensuring adequate headroom for
    # several more turns before compaction is needed again.
    target_utilization: 0.70

    # Minimum turns between compaction runs (prevents thrashing)
    cooldown_turns: 3

    # Time budget per normal compaction run (milliseconds)
    # Acts as a safety net — primary stop is goal achievement.
    # Philosophy: thorough compaction once > repeated tiny runs.
    max_duration_ms: 45000

    # Time budget for critical compaction (milliseconds)
    # Used when utilization exceeds critical_threshold.
    critical_max_duration_ms: 60000

    # Turn summarization: min turns before summarizing
    min_turns_to_summarize: 5

    # Turn summarization: max turns per summary batch
    max_turns_per_summary: 15

    # Recency window: protect the N most recent turns from compaction
    # These turns stay as raw history for conversational continuity
    compaction_recency_window: 5

    # Insight deduplication: merge redundant insights
    insight_dedup_enabled: true
    insight_similarity_threshold: 0.90
    max_insights_to_check: 50

    # Number of recent turns for utilization trend tracking
    trend_window: 10

  # On session startup, prime the context with knowledge from prior sessions.
  # This creates continuity even when episodic history is empty.
  #
  # Recency-Based Priming:
  # 1. Get top entities by hit_count (Hebbian importance)
  # 2. Fetch most recent insights from vector store (sorted by created_at)
  # 3. Fetch most recent summaries from vector store (sorted by created_at)

  # SUPPORTING CONTEXT BUDGET CONFIGURATION
  # =============================================================================
  # Controls how the token budget is split between supporting context
  # (insights, summaries, passages, etc.) and conversation history.
  #
  # The problem this solves:
  #   Budget is enforced during memory retrieval (_apply_budget), but significant
  #   content is added AFTER budget checks during prompt formatting
  #   (_build_supporting_context). This can cause prompts to exceed the
  #   configured context_window.
  #
  # How it works:
  #   1. Dynamic budget = context_window - system_prompt - tools - output_buffer
  #   2. Supporting context budget = dynamic_budget * budget_ratio
  #   3. Sections are built in section_priority order
  #   4. When budget is exhausted, remaining sections are truncated/omitted
  #
  # =============================================================================
  supporting_context:
    # Percentage of available budget allocated to supporting context (0.0-1.0)
    # Remaining budget goes to conversation history.
    # Higher ratio = more supporting context, less history
    # Lower ratio = less supporting context, more history
    budget_ratio: 0.25  # Increased for cross-session continuity

    # Priority order for sections when truncating (first = highest priority)
    # Sections are built in this order; when budget runs out, remaining
    # sections are skipped. If a section only partially fits, it's truncated.
    #
    # Available sections:
    #   - known_facts: Relationship summaries from graph store (nodes/edges)
    #   - passages: Semantic search results from vector store
    #   - insights: Rich contextual observations with timestamps
    #   - summaries: Conversation summaries (prior sessions)
    #   - tools: Tool recommendations and usage hints
    #   - state: Session state variables
    section_priority:

      - insights
      - summaries
      - tools
      - passages
      - state

  # =============================================================================

  # =============================================================================
  # PROMPT CACHING CONFIGURATION
  # =============================================================================
  # Controls prompt caching optimization for LLM providers that support it.
  # When enabled, the prompt layout is reordered to maximize cache hit rates.
  #
  # How LLM Caching Works:
  #   - Providers cache a PREFIX of the prompt (from the start)
  #   - Subsequent requests with the same prefix get cache hits
  #   - Cache hits reduce latency and cost significantly
  #
  # Cache-Optimized Layout (when enabled):
  #   1. System prompt (stable)
  #   2. Tool definitions (stable)
  #   3. Static context (insights, key facts - stable within session)
  #   4. Conversation history (grows but prefix is stable)
  #   ── CACHE BREAKPOINT ──
  #   5. Query-specific context (vector search results - volatile)
  #   6. Current user message
  #
  # Default Layout (when disabled):
  #   Optimized for "Lost in the Middle" attention patterns instead.
  #   Supporting context placed near query for recency effect.
  #
  # Provider Support:
  #   - anthropic: Explicit cache_control markers (best support)
  #   - openai: Automatic prefix caching (no markers needed)
  #   - auto: Detect provider from model name
  # =============================================================================
  cache:
    # Enable/disable cache-optimized prompt layout (default: false)
    # When false, uses attention-optimized layout (recency effect)
    enabled: false

    # Provider for cache control markers
    # Options: "auto", "anthropic", "openai", "none"
    # "auto" detects from model name (recommended)
    provider: "auto"

    # Cache breakpoint strategy
    # Options:
    #   "after_history" - Cache system + tools + static context + history
    #   "after_static"  - Cache system + tools + static context only
    #   "system_only"   - Cache only system prompt
    breakpoint: "after_history"

    # Include static context (insights, key facts) in cacheable prefix
    # When true, insights/facts are moved BEFORE history for better caching
    # When false, they stay in the final message (attention-optimized)
    static_context_in_prefix: true

    # Minimum conversation turns before enabling cache optimization
    # Short conversations may not benefit from caching overhead
    min_turns_for_cache: 3

    # TTL hint for Anthropic cache (seconds, 0 = provider default)
    # Anthropic default is 5 minutes
    ttl_seconds: 0

  priming:
    enabled: true              # Enable/disable automatic priming
    top_entities: 50          # Increased (indexed retrieval now efficient)
    max_insights: 20           # Cross-session knowledge (was 15)
    max_summaries: 15          # Conversation context (was 10)
    max_known_facts: 50        # Graph relationship summaries cap
    # max_facts removed — key_facts pipeline eliminated in favor of Known Facts (graph-based)
    recency_days: 30           # Wider window for continuity (was 14)
    # IMPORTANT: This budget should be LESS than supporting_context budget
    # supporting_context gets: (context_window - fixed_costs) * budget_ratio
    # With 40K context, ~4K fixed costs: (40K - 4K) * 0.25 = ~9K
    # Set priming lower to leave room for formatting overhead
    token_budget: 4000         # ~10% of context window (leaves headroom)

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # CROSS-SESSION HISTORY
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Include conversation turns from recent sessions for continuity.
    # This provides raw conversation context beyond just extracted insights.
    #
    # How it works:
    #   - On each recall(), fetch turns from the N most recent sessions
    #   - Turns are merged with current session history, ordered chronologically
    #   - Each turn displays with a timestamp prefix: [YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM]
    #   - Prior session turns have lower budget priority (dropped first)
    #
    # Use cases:
    #   - Continuing interrupted conversations
    #   - Providing context for follow-up questions across sessions
    #   - Maintaining conversational tone and topic continuity
    #
    # Trade-offs:
    #   - Higher values use more tokens but provide richer context
    #   - Set to 0 to disable and rely only on extracted insights/facts
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------

    # Number of prior sessions to include (0 = disabled)
    # Example: 2 means include turns from the 2 most recent sessions
    previous_sessions: 2

    # Maximum turns to include per prior session
    # Example: 5 means up to 5 turns from each prior session
    # Total prior turns = previous_sessions * previous_session_turns
    # WARNING: Prior history BYPASSES supporting_context budget!
    # Each turn is ~150-300 tokens. Keep this conservative.
    previous_session_turns: 8
